scenes.narration: The life of John Howard begins far from where the story usually starts. John Winston Howard (born 26 July 1939) is an Australian former politician who served as the 25th prime minister of Australia from 1996 to 2007, holding office as leader of the Liberal Party of Australia. His eleven-year tenure as prime minister is the second-longest in Australian history, after that of Robert Menzies.

John Howard was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. Howard was born in Sydney and studied law at the University of Sydney. A former federal president of the Young Liberals, he first stood for office at the 1968 New South Wales state election, but lost narrowly.

To understand where John Howard ended up, start with where John Howard began. At the 1974 federal election, Howard was elected as a member of parliament (MP) for the division of Bennelong. He was promoted to cabinet in 1977, and later in the year replaced Phillip Lynch as treasurer of Australia, remaining in that position until the defeat of Malcolm Fraser's government at the 1983 election.

The road from the beginning to the peak of John Howard ran through years nobody filmed. In 1985, Howard was elected leader of the Liberal Party for the first time, thus replacing Andrew Peacock as Leader of the Opposition. He led the Liberal–National coalition to the 1987 federal election, but lost to Bob Hawke's Labor government, and was removed from the leadership in 1989.

Each stage of the life of John Howard made the next stage possible. Remaining a key figure in the party, Howard was re-elected leader in 1995, replacing Alexander Downer, and subsequently led the Coalition to a landslide victory at the 1996 federal election. In his first term, Howard introduced reformed gun laws in response to the Port Arthur massacre, and controversially implemented a nationwide value-added tax, breaking a pre-election promise.

The people who knew John Howard young describe someone already restless. The Howard government called a snap election for October 1998, which they won, albeit with a greatly reduced majority. Going into the 2001 election, the Coalition trailed behind Labor in opinion polling.

What John Howard built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. However, in a campaign dominated by national security, Howard introduced changes to Australia's immigration system to deter asylum seekers from entering the country, and pledged military assistance to the United States following the September 11 attacks. Due to this, Howard won widespread support, and his government was narrowly re-elected.

By the time John Howard reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. In Howard's third term in office, Australia contributed troops to the War in Afghanistan and the Iraq War, and led the International Force for East Timor. In his final term in office, his government introduced industrial relations reforms known as  WorkChoices, which proved controversial and unpopular with the public.

The rise of John Howard was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. The Howard government was defeated at the 2007 federal election, with the Labor Party's Kevin Rudd succeeding him as prime minister. Howard also lost his own seat of Bennelong at the election to Maxine McKew, becoming only the second prime minister to do so, after Stanley Bruce at the 1929 election.

Setbacks came early for John Howard, and the response to them is the real story. Following this loss, Howard retired from politics, but has remained active in political discourse. Howard's government presided over a sustained period of economic growth and a large "mining boom", and significantly reduced government debt by the time he left office.

The legacy of John Howard outlived the circumstances that produced it. He was known for his broad appeal to voters across the political spectrum, and commanded a diverse base of supporters, colloquially referred to as his "battlers". His critics have admonished him for involving Australia in the Iraq War, his policies regarding asylum seekers, and his economic agenda.

Few lives travel as far as that of John Howard, and the distance is the point. Nonetheless, he has been frequently ranked within the upper-tier of Australian prime ministers by political experts and the general public. John Winston Howard is the fourth son of Mona (née Kell; 1899–1983) and Lyall Howard (1896–1955), an engineer, proprietor, and World War I veteran.

The childhood of John Howard contains the adult in small print. Howard's middle name "Winston" was given by his parents in honor of Prime Minister Winston Churchill. He is descended from convict William Tooley, who was transported to New South Wales in 1816 for stealing a watch.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of John Howard — in that order. Howard was born and raised in the Sydney suburb of Earlwood, in a Methodist family, and was also known as "Jack" in his youth. His mother had been an office worker until her marriage, while his father and his paternal grandfather, Walter Howard, were both veterans of the First Australian Imperial Force in the First World War.

The turning point in the life of John Howard looked like a failure at the time. In 1955, when he 16 years old, his father died, leaving his mother to take care of him. Howard suffered a hearing impairment in his youth, leaving him with a slight speech impediment, and he continues to wear a hearing aid.

Every biography of John Howard has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. It also influenced him in subtle ways, limiting his early academic performance; encouraging a reliance on an excellent memory; and in his mind ruling out becoming a barrister as a likely career. He won a citizenship prize in his final year at Earlwood (presented by local politician Eric Willis), and subsequently represented his secondary school at debating as well as cricket and rugby union.

The education of John Howard happened mostly outside any school. In his final year at school he took part in a radio show hosted by Jack Davey, Give It a Go, broadcast on the commercial radio station, 2GB. After gaining his Leaving Certificate, he studied law at the University of Sydney, graduating with a Bachelor of Laws degree in 1962.

What John Howard wanted at the start and what John Howard got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Howard began working for the firm of Stephen Jaques and Stephen (now Mallesons) as a junior solicitor. In 1964, he took a trip around the world, visiting Britain, Europe, Israel, India, and Singapore.

The defining trait of John Howard was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. After returning to Sydney in 1965, he began working for Clayton Utz, but "lacked the university grades and the social connections to be on track for a partnership". He subsequently moved to a smaller firm, which became Truman, Nelson and Howard after he was made a partner.

Those who met John Howard at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. He was a member of the party's New South Wales state executive and was federal president of the Young Liberals (the party youth organisation) from 1962 to 1964. Howard supported Australia's involvement in the Vietnam War, although has since said there were "aspects of it that could have been handled and explained differently".

The private years of John Howard explain the public decades better than any speech. At the 1963 federal election, Howard acted as campaign manager for Tom Hughes in his local seat of Parkes. In mid-1964, Howard travelled to London to work and travel for a period.

The family John Howard came from matters more than the legends admit. He volunteered for the Conservative Party in the electorate of Holborn and St Pancras South at the 1964 UK general election. In 1967, with the support of party power brokers John Carrick and Eric Willis, Howard was endorsed as candidate for the marginal suburban state seat of Drummoyne, held by Labor's Reg Coady.

The first real success of John Howard arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. Howard's mother sold the family home in Earlwood and rented a house with him at Five Dock, a suburb within the electorate. At the election in February 1968, in which the incumbent state Liberal government was returned to office, Howard narrowly lost to Coady, despite campaigning vigorously.

The last chapter of John Howard was written long after the fame. At the 1974 federal election, Howard successfully contested the Division of Bennelong, located in suburban Sydney. Howard supported Malcolm Fraser for the leadership of the Liberal Party against Billy Snedden following the 1974 election.

The whole life of John Howard reads like a single decision repeated. When Fraser won office at the 1975 federal election, Howard was appointed Minister for Business and Consumer Affairs, a position in which he served until 1977. At this stage, he followed the protectionist and pro-regulation stance of Fraser and the Liberal Party.

Between the birth and the legend of John Howard lie the years that actually decide it. In December 1977, aged 38, Howard was appointed Treasurer, in place of Phillip Lynch. Fraser said in his memoirs that he appointed him despite his limited experience because "he was bright and he got across a brief well, and he was a good manager".

The reputation of John Howard was built in the middle, not at the edges. During his five years in the position, Howard became an adherent of free-market economics, which was challenging economic orthodoxies in place for most of the century. He came to favour tax reform including broad-based taxation (later the GST), a freer industrial system including the dismantling of the centralised wage-fixing system, the abolition of compulsory trade unionism, privatisation and deregulation.

Somebody like John Howard should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. In 1978, the Fraser government instigated the Campbell Committee to investigate financial system reforms. Howard supported the Campbell report, but adopted an incremental approach with Cabinet, as there was wide opposition to deregulation within the government and the treasury.

The life of John Howard begins far from where the story usually starts. The process of reform began before the committee reported 21⁄2 years later, with the introduction of the tender system for the sale of Treasury notes in 1979, and Treasury bonds in 1982. Ian Macfarlane described these reforms as "second only in importance to the float of the Australian dollar in 1983." In 1981, Howard proposed a broad-based indirect tax with compensatory cuts in personal rates; however, cabinet rejected it citing both inflationary and political reasons.

John Howard was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. After the free-marketeers or "drys" of the Liberals challenged the protectionist policies of Minister for Industry and Commerce Phillip Lynch, they shifted their loyalties to Howard. Following an unsuccessful leadership challenge by Andrew Peacock to unseat Fraser as prime minister, Howard was elected deputy leader of the Liberal Party in April 1982.

To understand where John Howard ended up, start with where John Howard began. His election depended largely on the support of the "drys", and he became the party's champion of the growing free-market lobby. The economic crises of the early 1980s brought Howard into conflict with the Keynesian Fraser.

The road from the beginning to the peak of John Howard ran through years nobody filmed. As the economy headed towards the worst recession since the 1930s, Fraser pushed an expansionary fiscal position much to Howard's and Treasury's horror. With his authority as treasurer being flouted, Howard considered resigning in July 1982, but, after discussions with his wife and senior advisor John Hewson, he decided to "tough it out".

Each stage of the life of John Howard made the next stage possible. The 1982 wages explosion—wages rose 16 per cent across the country—resulted in stagflation; unemployment touched double-digits and inflation peaked at 12.5% (official interest rates peaked at 21%). The Fraser government with Howard as Treasurer lost the 1983 election to the Labor Party led by Bob Hawke.

The people who knew John Howard young describe someone already restless. Over the course of the 1980s, the Liberal Party came to accept the free-market policies that Fraser had resisted and Howard had espoused. Policies included low protection, decentralisation of wage fixation, financial deregulation, a broadly based indirect tax, and the rejection of counter-cyclical fiscal policy.
